name: Verdejo

lines.s10: Verdejo is the bright, fennel scented white of Rueda, on the high plateau of Castile, with lime, grapefruit and a gently bitter finish.
lines.s20: Verdejo is the white grape of Rueda, on the high plateau of Castile, where it is picked at night to keep it fresh. It tastes of lime, grapefruit and fennel, dry and brisk, and it ends on a faint, pleasing bitterness.
lines.s45: Verdejo is picked in the dark. It is the white grape of Rueda, on the high, stony plateau north west of Madrid, and the cold night air keeps its scent fresh. It tastes of lime, grapefruit and white peach, with fennel, cut grass and a faintly bitter finish. It is dry and medium bodied, with brisk acidity. Most is made cold in steel and sold young, and a few richer bottles are raised in barrel. It suits grilled fish, asparagus or goat's cheese. For centuries Rueda made a golden, nutty wine from it, aged like Sherry, and the fresh style in your glass is the newcomer.
lines.sale: Verdejo does what Sauvignon Blanc does and adds fennel and a bitter twist that sharpens the appetite. Try it with the shrimp remoulade, or with asparagus and a salad of goat's cheese.

glass.lead: Lime, grapefruit and white peach with fennel, bay leaf and cut grass, dry and brisk, closing on a faint note of bitter almond.

ladder.where: Rueda's high plateau, with hot days and cold nights
La Mancha, on the warm central plain

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol moderate, body medium, with a slightly oily feel and a faint bitterness on the finish; rarely any new oak.

home.home: Rueda, on the high, dry plateau of Castilla y León, where the vines stand on stony gravel and summer nights are cold. The grapes are picked at night and made cold in steel, because the juice browns quickly in heat and air. A bottle that names Verdejo is at least 85 per cent the grape.
home.abroad: It has barely left Spain. La Mancha grows it for fresh, grassy whites, and beyond Spain it is a rarity.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius: well chilled.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; open it cold and pour.
service.age: Young, within a year or two; barrel fermented and old vine bottles keep a few years more.

labels.means: The denomination in Castilla y León; a bottle that names Verdejo is at least 85 per cent the grape.
On the lees: a fuller Verdejo kept on its spent yeast.
Barrel fermented: a richer, rounder style that can age.
A mark for wines from vineyards over 30 years old, cropped low.
Rueda's historic golden wine, aged in air until nutty, in the manner of Sherry.

guest.a: Close. It is as crisp and as green, but where Sauvignon Blanc is all gooseberry and cut grass, Verdejo adds fennel, bay leaf and a faint bitter finish, with a little more body.

guest.q: Why does it finish slightly bitter?
guest.a: That is the grape's signature, a gentle bitterness like almond skin or fennel. It is meant to be there, and it is part of why the wine sits so well with food.

guest.q: Is Verdejo the same as Verdelho?
guest.a: No. Verdelho is a grape of Madeira and is unrelated. Verdejo belongs to Rueda, on the high plateau in the centre of Spain.

compare.tell: Sauvignon Blanc shows gooseberry and cut grass more loudly, with sharper acidity; Verdejo is a little rounder, with fennel, bay leaf and a bitter finish.
Albariño is white peach and apricot with a salty finish and no bite of bay leaf; Verdejo is greener, with lime and fennel.
Macabeo, Rueda's Viura, is quieter and more neutral, with green apple and almond; Verdejo is louder and greener, and more bitter on the finish.

cards.front: Verdejo: where is home, and why is it harvested at night?
cards.back: Rueda, on the high plateau of Castilla y León. The juice browns and loses its scent in heat and air, so the fruit is picked in the cold of night and made cold in steel.

cards.front: Verdejo blind: what parts it from Sauvignon Blanc?
cards.back: Fennel, bay leaf and a faint bitter almond finish on a slightly rounder, oilier body. Sauvignon Blanc shows gooseberry and cut grass more loudly, with sharper acidity.

cards.front: What are Rueda's two historic aged wines, and how do they differ?
cards.back: Dorado is aged in air, golden and nutty. Pálido is aged under flor, the veil of yeast, and stays pale. Both recall Sherry.

questions.q: A blind white is pale straw with green glints, dry and unoaked: lime, grapefruit, fennel and bay leaf, high acidity, a slightly oily feel and a faint bitter finish. Which grape and origin fit it?
questions.exp: Fennel, bay leaf and a bitter finish on a slightly oily texture mark Verdejo. Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc would be louder, with passion fruit and gooseberry and no bitter twist.

questions.q: A guest reads on the back label of her Rueda that the grapes were harvested at night, and asks why. What is the reason?
opts: Cool fruit keeps its scent and does not brown
Night picking raises the sugar in the grapes
The rules forbid picking by day
Dew on the grapes lowers the alcohol
questions.exp: Verdejo browns and loses its aromatics with heat and air, so Rueda picks in the cold of the night and works cold in the cellar. Sugar does not rise at night.

questions.q: A guest orders a Rueda that names Verdejo on its label and asks how much of the grape the bottle must hold. What do you answer?
questions.exp: A Rueda that names the grape is at least 85 per cent Verdejo. A plain Rueda needs only half, with other permitted whites such as Viura making up the rest.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Rueda, with La Mancha as the one other place the Codex names for the grape.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials and the region record for Rueda supplied the fruit (lime, grapefruit, white peach, melon rind), fennel, bay leaf and cut grass, the bitter finish, the oily feel, the night harvest, the 85 and 50 per cent labels, Gran Vino de Rueda, Dorado and Pálido and the trap of Verdelho.
The fresh style as the newcomer rests on the Codex's own record of the move of 1972; the golden, aged wine of earlier centuries on the Rueda council's history and on Foods and Wines from Spain.
The tradition that the grape reached the Duero with settlers in the eleventh century is given by the council and by Foods and Wines from Spain as likely, not documented; it was left out of the entry.

The warm rung of the ladder (La Mancha: melon rind, ripe peach) is a taster's reading of what warmth does to the grape; the Codex's region record says only that La Mancha makes aromatic, grassy whites from it. Nectarine beside white peach, and toasted hazelnut for the barrel fermented wines, are likewise a taster's reading.
The reviewed profile's confuse line uses the word pyrazine; the entry says gooseberry and cut grass, as the brief asks of a spoken line.
The shrimp remoulade is the one dish from the Creole table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
